routes.description: Establish early individual and group appearance testimony, interpret it as bodily resurrection testimony, and compare resurrection with naturalistic alternatives under historical explanatory criteria.
routes.successCriteria: The reported death, appearances, conversions, bodily-resurrection belief, and resulting movement must be sufficiently supported and collectively better expected under resurrection than under the proposed natural explanations.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus rose and that resurrection explains the early Christian testimony more adequately than the available naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early, apostolically connected sources report appearances to individuals and groups.
Establish that the relevant testimony concerns Jesus's transformed physical body rather than visions alone.
Show that hallucination, contagion, legendary development, and related natural mechanisms do not adequately explain the reported evidence.
Apply explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of unsupported assumptions to the competing hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Integrate Jesus's prior claims, reported deeds, prediction, appearances, conversions, and the resulting movement into the comparison.
Preserve the historical usefulness of the Gospel core despite literary shaping and peripheral differences.

routes.description: Require evidence proportionate to resurrection's low background probability and explain the testimony through established psychological, social, and literary processes.
routes.successCriteria: The surviving testimony must remain insufficiently exceptional to overcome resurrection's prior burden while visions, social contagion, missing-body scenarios, and tradition development remain adequate natural possibilities.

motionBridge.description: Show that the early Christian testimony does not warrant resurrection over established natural classes of explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that an unprecedented divine resurrection requires exceptionally strong confirming evidence.
Explain individual and group appearance beliefs through culturally conditioned visions, suggestion, and charismatic contagion.
Show that the early epistolary evidence lacks the detail needed to establish shared encounters with a physical Jesus or verification of an empty grave.
Account for detailed resurrection narratives through legendary growth, redaction, literary imitation, and mythmaking.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that loss, removal, or nonverification of a body can accompany appearance beliefs without resurrection.
Compare the reported narrow appearance pattern with what a local visionary movement and a universally revealing deity would predict.

sectionSelections.title: Historical Method and Prior Probability
sectionSelections.rationale: The governing comparison depends on whether explanatory criteria can bracket resurrection's prior probability or whether its lack of established precedent imposes an exceptional evidential burden.

proSelections.proposition: Historical hypotheses should be compared by explanatory scope, explanatory power, avoidance of unsupported assumptions, and plausibility against accepted facts.
Because resurrection reference classes and prior probabilities are disputed or inscrutable, historians should bracket the prior and compare how likely the evidence is under each hypothesis.

conSelections.proposition: Because resurrection lacks established background precedent, it is an extraordinary claim requiring much stronger evidence than the testimony presented.
Plausibility corresponds to prior probability, so a hypothesis invoking unestablished causes requires exceptionally strong evidence that the resurrection case lacks.

sectionSelections.title: Early Testimony and Bodily Resurrection
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether the earliest evidence reports apostolically connected encounters with a transformed physical Jesus or sparse and culturally conditioned visionary experiences.

proSelections.proposition: Paul preserves early testimony connected with the Jerusalem apostles that Jesus appeared after his death to individuals and groups.
Paul's resurrection teaching concerns Jesus's transformed physical corpse, and resurrection is offered as the explanation of the reported individual and group appearances.

conSelections.proposition: Rapidly developing miracle traditions and older resurrection and apotheosis narratives make the Christian resurrection story susceptible to legendary construction.
Paul's letters depict vision-prone Christian communities and do not establish that the appearances were detailed, shared encounters with a physically risen Jesus.

sectionSelections.title: Psychological and Group-Appearance Mechanisms
sectionSelections.rationale: A principal clash concerns whether known psychological and social processes can generate the reported individual and group experiences and the ensuing bodily-resurrection belief.

proSelections.proposition: The apostles' social, marital, and missionary behavior conflicts with the proposed schizotypal profile and weakens that hallucination explanation.
Reported ordinary-state features and the resulting belief in bodily resurrection with an empty grave make altered-state hallucinations an inadequate explanation.

conSelections.proposition: Cognitive dissonance is a testable explanatory hypothesis rather than a clinical diagnosis and is inherently likelier than a divine apparition absent strong contrary evidence.
The appearance sequence can be explained through a private vision followed by charismatic suggestion and progressively larger ecstatic group experiences.

sectionSelections.title: Cumulative Explanatory Comparison
sectionSelections.rationale: The central inference requires comparing how the resurrection and naturalistic routes account for the combined reports rather than treating each appearance, conversion, or missing-body claim in isolation.

proSelections.proposition: Jesus's religious claims, reputed miracles, resurrection prediction, and reported appearances to friends, foes, individuals, and groups create a cumulative context stronger than a merely missing body.
Resurrection explains the reported individual and group appearances, conversions, and Christian movement better than the hallucination hypothesis under the stated historical criteria.

conSelections.proposition: Combining rare missing-body and appearance reports does not favor resurrection because their natural causes remain jointly more probable than supernatural causes.
Sparse epistolary evidence is not exceptional enough to overcome resurrection's low prior probability, while culturally conditioned visions can explain the early Christian beliefs.

sectionSelections.title: Gospel Literary and Historical Value
sectionSelections.rationale: The detailed bodily and empty-tomb narratives depend partly on whether Gospel composition and disagreement preserve a usable historical core or instead indicate literary and legendary development.

proSelections.proposition: Mark consistently anticipates Jesus's resurrection, and its abrupt ending is plausibly incomplete rather than evidence of a non-resurrection Christian tradition.
Ancient biographical freedom and contradictions in peripheral details do not discredit the core Gospel account.

conSelections.proposition: Mark's composition of a resurrection story does not establish its historical truth, and an intentional ending remains compatible with anticipated visions outside the narrative.
Externally contradicted phenomena, implausible narratives, redactional embellishment, literary imitation, and inter-Gospel contradictions indicate mythmaking rather than historical reliability.
